bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Coastal Plain Oil and Gas Leasing Program Record of Decision.

industries.rationale: The bill directly expands the acreage available for oil and gas leasing and development in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
Environmental and conservation organizations have a direct stake in decisions affecting protected wildlife refuge lands and resource extraction policies.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would reverse a December 2024 decision by the Bureau of Land Management that restricted oil and gas leasing in Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. The 2024 decision made about 1.2 million acres unavailable for leasing while keeping the legally required minimum of 400,000 acres open. If this resolution passes, it would nullify those restrictions and revert to a 2020 framework that made the full 1.6 million acres of the Coastal Plain available for oil and gas development.

bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to "National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision".
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

industries.rationale: The resolution would reopen approximately 48% of the National Petroleum Reserve to oil and gas leasing, directly expanding access for extraction companies.
Environmental and conservation organizations have a direct stake in the wildlife and subsistence protections that would be removed by reverting to the 2020 plan.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would cancel a 2022 federal land-management plan for the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska and restore the previous 2020 plan. The 2022 plan closed roughly half of the 23-million-acre reserve to oil and gas leasing to protect wildlife and subsistence uses. Reversing it would reopen those areas to energy development under the earlier rules.

industries.rationale: Designation of critical environmental concern areas on federal land typically restricts oil and gas leasing and extraction activities.
Resource management plan designations directly affect mineral extraction rights and mining operations on federal lands.
Environmental and conservation organizations have direct stakes in land-use designations and protected-area classifications.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify a Bureau of Land Management rule issued in November 2024 that governs how approximately 3.6 million acres of federal land in Alaska's Central Yukon area are managed. The BLM rule designated 21 areas as critical environmental concern or research natural areas. If passed, the resolution would cancel that rule and prevent it from taking effect.

bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Public Land Order No. 7917 for Withdrawal of Federal Lands; Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, MN.

industries.rationale: The bill would directly reopen over 225,000 acres to mineral exploration and leasing that are currently withdrawn from such activity.
The bill affects protections for wilderness areas and watersheds, directly implicating environmental and conservation advocacy organizations.
The bill would reopen the lands to geothermal energy leasing and development alongside mineral leasing.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would reverse a federal order that withdrew approximately 225,504 acres of national forest land in northeastern Minnesota from mineral and geothermal leasing. The original order, issued in 2023, was intended to protect the Rainy River Watershed and the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness from potential mining impacts for 20 years. If passed, the resolution would reopen these lands to mineral exploration and development, as well as geothermal energy leasing.

bill.title: To reduce trawl gear impacts on bycatch and seafloor habitat in the Bering Sea, Aleutian Islands, and Gulf of Alaska, to establish gear performance standards, seafloor contact detection, and salmon excluder requirements, to improve Council transparency and participation, to prioritize ecosystem analyses, to modernize electronic monitoring, to prohibit unsustainable foreign seafood imports, and to establish a Bycatch Mitigation and Habitat Protection Assistance Fund.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates commercial fishing gear, bycatch standards, and seafood imports, imposing new compliance costs and operational requirements on the fishing sector.
The prohibition on certain foreign seafood imports would affect seafood retailers and distributors who source products from international suppliers.
The electronic monitoring and seafloor contact detection requirements would create demand for specialized monitoring technology and data systems in fishing operations.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would impose new requirements on commercial fishing operations in Alaska waters, including standards for trawl gear to reduce bycatch and seafloor damage, mandatory salmon excluder devices, and seafloor contact detection systems. It would also establish electronic monitoring requirements, ban imports of certain foreign seafood deemed unsustainable, and create a fund to help fisheries comply with bycatch and habitat protection measures. The bill additionally mandates ecosystem impact analyses and changes to fishery management council procedures.

bill.title: HALT Fentanyl Act
bill.latestActionText: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill changes registration and licensing requirements for pharmaceutical researchers working with controlled substances and affects the regulatory classification of fentanyl-related compounds.
The bill establishes new criminal penalties and quantity thresholds that will affect defense attorneys and prosecutors handling drug trafficking cases.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would permanently classify all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, meaning they would be treated as having high abuse potential and no accepted medical use. It sets the same criminal penalties and quantity thresholds for fentanyl-related substances as currently apply to fentanyl analogues. The bill also creates a streamlined registration process for researchers studying Schedule I substances and makes it easier for registered researchers to conduct certain activities without additional permits.

bill.title: CLEAN Act
bill.latestActionText: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining. Hearings held.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects geothermal energy developers by increasing lease sale frequency and establishing permit response deadlines.
Electric utilities that generate power from geothermal sources would benefit from increased access to federal leases for development.
The bill involves leasing and drilling on federal land, activities that overlap with mining sector operations and regulatory frameworks.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would require the Department of the Interior to hold lease sales for geothermal energy development on federal land at least once a year in states where parcels have been nominated, instead of the current requirement of once every two years. It would also require Interior to offer all eligible nominated parcels at each sale and to hold a replacement sale in the same year if a sale is canceled or delayed. The bill sets deadlines for Interior to respond to applications for geothermal drilling permits.

districtAwards.description: STATE OF ALASKA RURAL HEALTH TRANSFORMATION PROGRAM - DESCRIPTIVE TITLE: ALASKA’S RURAL HEALTH TRANSFORMATION PROGRAM  ORGANIZATION NAME: STATE OF ALASKA DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH   SUBRECIPIENTS/SUB-AWARDEES: A WIDE RANGE OF ENTITIES ACROSS ALASKA WILL PARTICIPATE AS FUNDING SUBRECIPIENTS, INCLUDING: HEALTH CARE DELIVERY ORGANIZATIONS; TRIBAL HEALTH ORGANIZATIONS; COMMUNITY-BASED ENTITIES; EDUCATION AND WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT INSTITUTIONS; TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION VENDORS; PROVIDER AND TRADE ASSOCIATIONS; CONSULTING AND PROFESSIONAL SERVICES FIRMS; AND STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS OR AUTHORITIES ENGAGED IN PUBLIC HEALTH, EDUCATION, OR EMERGENCY MEDICAL RESPONSE.   PROJECT GOALS:    1. PROMOTE LIFELONG HEALTH AND WELL-BEING FOR RURAL, REMOTE, AND FRONTIER ALASKANS.    2. BUILD SUSTAINABLE, OUTCOMES-DRIVEN HEALTH SYSTEMS.    3. DRIVE WORKFORCE AND TECHNOLOGY INNOVATION.    TOTAL BUDGET AMOUNT: $1,000,000,000.00    BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF FUND USAGE: ALASKA PROPOSES TO USE RHTP FUNDING TO STRENGTHEN COMMUNITY-LED AND REGIONALLY DESIGNED HEALTH SYSTEMS THAT PROVIDE ACCESS TO A FULL CONTINUUM OF CARE AS CLOSE TO ALASKANS’ HOMES AS POSSIBLE. THE FUNDS WILL BE AWARDED TO ENTITIES TO LAUNCH PROJECTS IN SUPPORT OF ALASKA’S SIX INITIATIVES: (1) HEALTHY BEGINNINGS, WHICH STRENGTHENS MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH AS A FOUNDATION FOR HEALTHY FAMILIES; (2) HEALTH CARE ACCESS, WHICH EXPANDS AND SUSTAINS ESSENTIAL PRIMARY, BEHAVIORAL, ORAL, SPECIALTY, EMERGENCY, HOME AND COMMUNITY-BASED AND POST-ACUTE CARE HEALTH SERVICES ACROSS ALASKA’S RURAL COMMUNITIES; (3) HEALTHY COMMUNITIES, WHICH INVESTS IN ENHANCING ACCESS TO PREVENTIVE AND PRIMARY CARE SERVICES THAT ENABLE EARLY CHRONIC DISEASE MANAGEMENT, EXPANDING THE USE OF CONSUMER-FACING DIGITAL TOOLS AND POPULATION HEALTH CLINICAL INFRASTRUCTURE, AND PROMOTING HEALTHY LIFESTYLES WITH CULTURALLY APPROPRIATE COMMUNITY EDUCATION; (4) PAY FOR VALUE: FISCAL SUSTAINABILITY, WHICH INCENTIVIZES A SHIFT FROM TRADITIONAL VOLUME-BASED REIMBURSEMENT MODELS TO BUILD THE LONG-TERM FINANCIAL STABILITY OF RURAL PROVIDERS THROUGH VOLUNTARY INNOVATIVE CARE AND PAYMENT MODELS THAT INCREASE CARE COORDINATION, LOWER COSTS AND IMPROVE HEALTH OUTCOMES; (5) STRENGTHEN WORKFORCE, WHICH BUILDS A RESILIENT RURAL HEALTH CARE WORKFORCE THROUGH PIPELINE, RECRUITMENT, TRAINING AND RETENTION STRATEGIES, ALONGSIDE WRAPAROUND HOUSING AND CHILD CARE SUPPORTS TO HELP PROVIDERS REMAIN IN RURAL COMMUNITIES; AND (6) SPARK TECHNOLOGY AND INNOVATION, WHICH HARNESSES DATA AND TECHNOLOGY TO EXPAND THE USE OF CONSUMER WEARABLES AND DIGITAL DEVICES, ENHANCE TELEHEALTH, FOSTER APPROPRIATE USE OF AI, STRENGTHEN CYBERSECURITY, FACILITATE DATA SHARING AND SYSTEM INTEROPERABILITY, AND TEST NEW DELIVERY MODALITIES USING EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES. THESE SIX INITIATIVES ARE FLEXIBLE, PHASED, AND VOLUNTARY, ALLOWING EACH COMMUNITY AND PROVIDER TO ENGAGE AT A PACE AND SCALE SUITED TO THEIR LOCAL PRIORITIES AND RESOURCES. THESE INITIATIVES WILL TRANSFORM ALASKA’S HEALTH SYSTEM. THEY REFLECT ALASKA’S CULTURE OF INNOVATION AND SELF-RELIANCE, AND AFFIRM OUR COMMITMENT TO HIGH-QUALITY, ACCESSIBLE, AND SUSTAINABLE CARE.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
